newsitem.title: UK: Labour win is proof new polling methods work in UK.
newsitem.headline: Labour win is proof new polling methods work in UK.

text.p: Professional pollsters breathed a sigh of relief as five years of uncertainty over political polling methods came to an end with the landslide victory for Labour in Britain's election.

"The polls have been vindicated and they are not as John Major(former Prime Minister) said -- rubbish," said Bob Wybrow, Director at polling organisation Gallup. "We learned from the 1992 experience and have updated our methods."
The results so far, give Labour 45 percent share of the vote, Conservatives 31 percent and the Liberal Democrats 17 percent.
Most of the results from polling organisations are within one to three percent of the final outcome projected by analysts.
"Even with a perfect sample, the laws of statistics say the margin of error could be three to four percent," said Wybrow.
In the 1979, 1983 and 1987 opinion polls were fairly accurate in projections of political support.
But in April 1992, the Conservatives won a fourth term with a 21-seat majority, even though most opinion polls had consistently forecast a Labour victory.
After the experience of the last election, the Market Research Society (MRS) set up a committee of pollsters, academics and market researchers to pinpoint the reasons for the discrepancy.

The study, carried out over two years, came up with the conclusion that the failure of opinion polls in 1992 was due to inadequacies in sampling and the late swing towards the Conservatives among the "don't knows".
A third major reason given by the MRS was the higher likelihood of Conservative supporters hiding their loyalties. Labour supporters, it said, were less likely to hide their preferences.
Changes to techniques, particularly to account for those who hide their intentions have been made. The most successful this time round was ICM with a two percent error margin.
The final ICM poll forecast 33 percent support for the Conservatives, 43 percent for Labour and 18 percent for the Liberal Democrats.

"It's largely down to our adjustment mechanism. The don't knows and refusals were readjusted back to the party they voted for in the last election," said Stephen Ogborn, senior research executive at ICM.
Research from the results of the 1992 election found 60 percent of people who said they did not know who they would vote for, turned out for the party they had supported in 1987.
ICM reallocated 60 percent of the current "don't knows" back to the party they voted for in 1992, said Nick Sparrow, managing director at ICM.
Pollsters use different methods and have made various different adjustments for closet Conservatives.

"But there is not a huge difference between the final polls. It shows that adjusting for shy Conservatives was the right thing to do," said Nick Moon director of political research at polling organisation NOP.
